title: Ordering that survives a dead signal
summary: Warung owners lost a whole order every time the 3G dropped mid-basket.
scope: Team of 5 · I owned sync and conflict resolution
problem: Roughly 38% of our sellers are on 3G or worse for part of the day. The app assumed a live connection, so a dropped signal at checkout lost the basket. Sellers learned not to trust it and went back to a notebook, which meant our stock numbers were fiction.
approach: Rewrote the client as offline-first with a local queue and last-write-wins on a per-line basis rather than per-order, because two staff adding different items to the same order is normal in a warung and should not be a conflict. Server keeps a 72-hour idempotency window so a retry after a long outage does not duplicate. We shipped a deliberately boring sync indicator - sellers needed to know it was safe, not that it was clever.
outcome: Order loss effectively stopped and stock accuracy recovered, which was the actual goal. The notebook is still there in most warung and probably always will be; we stopped fighting it.

details.value: Order loss 4.1% → 0.2% of sessions

details.value: 61,000 warung, 2.8M orders/month

details.value: Sync protocol, conflict resolution, idempotency window

title: Designing for sellers who do not read menus
summary: Our navigation assumed a literacy and a phone our sellers did not have.
problem: Activation was 71% in Jakarta and 29% outside Java. Session replays showed sellers hunting through a text menu on a 5-inch screen in daylight. Several were functionally low-literacy in Indonesian even though they spoke it fluently - the product had no path for them at all.
approach: Rebuilt the primary flows around product photos and numbers instead of labels, raised the minimum tap target to 56dp because the app is used one-handed while serving, and pushed contrast past AA because the phone is in direct sun most of the day. Added Javanese and Sundanese for the onboarding flow only, where the cost of misunderstanding is highest. Tested in actual warung, not in a lab.
outcome: The regional gap closed by more than half. The photo-first pattern was adopted across the seller app afterwards.

title: One ERP, six tax regimes, no forks
summary: Every new market had been a code fork. The seventh would have broken us.
scope: GPM · 4 squads across Singapore and Ho Chi Minh City
problem: Indonesian VAT, Malaysian SST, Vietnamese VAT, Thai WHT, Philippine EWT and Singapore GST had each been implemented as a branch of the invoicing module. Six forks meant every bug was fixed six times, and the Vietnam e-invoice mandate was going to need a seventh.
approach: Pushed hard for a rules engine with jurisdiction as data rather than code, which the team had wanted for two years and had never been funded. Bought the funding by tying it to the Vietnam mandate deadline rather than to engineering health, because that is the argument that wins. Migrated Singapore first - the simplest regime - so the abstraction was proven before it met Indonesian VAT.
outcome: Vietnam e-invoicing shipped as configuration. The honest caveat: Philippine EWT still has 200 lines of special-casing because the withholding matrix genuinely does not generalise, and we stopped pretending it would.

details.value: New tax regime 14 weeks → 9 days

details.value: Unblocked 3 markets, $2.1M contracted ARR

title: The Ramadan campaign we should not have sent
summary: Our biggest season, and the lifecycle programme was actively hurting it.
problem: Ramadan is 30-40% of annual warung turnover. Our re-engagement sequence fired on days-since-last-login, so in the busiest weeks of the year it was messaging the sellers who were too busy serving customers to open an app. Unsubscribes tripled every Ramadan and we had treated that as seasonal noise for three years.
approach: Re-keyed the whole programme to transaction volume instead of login recency, so a seller doing record numbers is left alone. Moved the sends to after Isya prayer, when sellers actually reconcile the day. Cut send volume by 60% and ran it as a proper holdout rather than shipping to everyone and comparing to last year.
outcome: Fewer sends, better numbers. The uncomfortable finding was that the previous three Ramadans of 'seasonal churn' were substantially self-inflicted.

details.value: Ramadan churn 8.9% → 3.4% (n = 41k)

details.value: Send volume down 60%, revenue per send up 4.1x

title: Catching Thai line-break bugs before customers did
summary: Thai has no spaces between words, and our test suite never noticed.
problem: Invoice PDFs were breaking Thai words mid-syllable, which ranges from unprofessional to genuinely unreadable. Every test fixture used Latin text, so the suite was green while customers were sending out broken documents. Two enterprise accounts raised it before we found it ourselves.
approach: Replaced every text fixture with real Thai, Lao and Khmer strings including the tone marks and the long compounds that break naive wrapping. Added a rendering assertion on the generated PDF rather than the DOM, because the bug only existed after typesetting. Kept a small Latin set purely as a control so a regression in the harness itself is visible.
outcome: The class of bug is now caught on the PR that introduces it. It also surfaced three existing rendering bugs nobody had reported - customers had just been working around them.

details.label: Escape rate
details.value: Script-rendering defects 9/quarter → 0 in 2 quarters

details.value: 3 unreported rendering bugs customers had worked around

title: Thai SMEs were not avoiding bookkeeping - they were avoiding us
summary: The roadmap said 'education'. The shop owners said something else.
problem: Only 12% of signups reached a first reconciled month. The prevailing internal theory was that Thai SMEs did not understand double-entry and needed tutorials, and a large education initiative was already scoped.
approach: Spent two days each with 16 shop owners in Bangkok, Khon Kaen and Chiang Mai. They understood their books perfectly - most kept immaculate paper ledgers. What they would not do is put revenue figures into a cloud product they suspected the Revenue Department could see. Nobody had asked about tax exposure because nobody on the team thought of it as a product problem.
outcome: The education initiative was cancelled. We shipped a local-only mode and explicit, plain-Thai documentation of exactly what is stored and who can request it. Activation moved for the first time in two years.

title: Same-day QRIS settlement for 300k merchants
summary: T+2 settlement was fine for Bank Indonesia and fatal for a warung.
scope: Team of 8 · I owned the settlement ledger
problem: QRIS acceptance was growing fast and our merchants were quietly going back to cash. A warung buys stock daily; money that arrives in two days is money they cannot trade with. Moving to same-day meant paying out before the interchange file arrived, which is a credit decision wearing an engineering costume.
approach: Built a double-entry ledger with an explicit float position per merchant, so the exposure was a number the risk team could see and cap rather than something hidden in a job. Payouts run continuously against that cap and reconcile against the BI-FAST file when it lands. We deliberately did not offer same-day to merchants under 60 days old, and took the churn.
outcome: Same-day is now the default for eligible merchants. Reconciliation breaks are rare and, more importantly, visible - the previous batch job used to swallow them.

details.label: Settlement
details.value: T+2 → same day for 81% of merchant volume

details.label: Correctness
details.value: 0 unexplained breaks across 74M settled transactions

details.label: Trade-off
details.value: No same-day under 60 days tenure - we accepted the churn

title: The two seconds before someone pays a stranger
summary: First-time QRIS payers abandoned at the amount screen, and they were right to.
problem: Abandonment on a first scan-to-pay was 34%. The screen showed a merchant name pulled straight from the QR payload - often an unrecognisable legal entity, sometimes just a registration number. People were being asked to send money to a name that did not match the shop they were standing in.
approach: Showed the trading name and the neighbourhood alongside the legal entity, because that is what a person can verify by looking up. Added an explicit 'this cannot be reversed' line, which tested better than any reassurance we tried - people want the risk stated, not softened. Tested three friction levels; the middle one won, the lightest felt unsafe.
outcome: Completion rose sharply and, unexpectedly, disputes fell - people were catching genuinely wrong merchants before paying rather than after.

details.value: First-scan completion 66% → 91%

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Wrong-merchant disputes down 47%

title: Making double-charges structurally impossible
summary: Retries on a flaky mobile network were creating real duplicate payments.
scope: Team of 4 · I owned the transfer core
problem: Vietnamese mobile connectivity is good until it is not, and client retries on an unacknowledged transfer were creating duplicates. We were refunding roughly 900 a month by hand. The existing dedupe was a Redis key with a TTL, which is fine until Redis fails over mid-flight - and it had.
approach: Moved idempotency into the same Postgres transaction as the ledger write, keyed on a client-generated reference, so a duplicate is a unique-constraint violation rather than a cache lookup. Slower per request and unambiguously correct, which is the right trade for money. Backfilled 18 months of history to find duplicates we had never noticed.
outcome: Manual refunds for duplicates went to zero. The backfill found 2,400 historical duplicates nobody had reported, which we refunded proactively.

details.value: ~900 manual duplicate refunds/month → 0

details.label: Found on arrival
details.value: 2,400 historical duplicates, refunded proactively

details.value: p99 transfer 240ms → 310ms - accepted for correctness

title: Surviving Tết without a war room
summary: Lunar New Year is 9x normal volume in a four-hour window, once a year.
problem: Tết eve transfer volume peaks at roughly nine times an ordinary evening, concentrated between 20:00 and midnight as people send lì xì. The previous two years needed the whole engineering team online, and the year before that we had a 40-minute outage at the worst possible moment.
approach: Stopped treating it as a capacity problem and started treating it as a queueing one: pre-scaled on a schedule rather than reactively, because autoscaling cannot react fast enough to a step function, and added explicit load shedding that degrades non-essential reads before it touches transfers. Ran a full-scale game day in November against production-shaped traffic.
outcome: Tết ran with two people on call and no incidents. Pre-scaling costs roughly $9k for the week, which is cheap against the alternative.

details.value: Tết peak handled at 9.4x baseline, zero incidents

title: Lending to people with no credit history
summary: Two thirds of applicants were invisible to a bureau-based model.
scope: Head of risk data · 4 analysts, 2 engineers
problem: SLIK coverage is thin for informal-sector workers, who are most of our target market. The bureau model rejected 68% of applicants for having no file, which is not a risk signal - it is an absence of one. Every proposed alternative signal was either unavailable or a proxy for something we are not allowed to price on.
approach: Built the model on cash-flow behaviour from the applicant's own e-wallet history, with explicit consent and a clear withdrawal path, rather than on device or social graph data. Ran it in shadow against the bureau model for six months before it decided anything. Fought for - and got - a fairness review across gender and province before launch, and we did drop two features that failed it.
outcome: Approval rose without default following it. The fairness review found a province-level disparity we would otherwise have shipped, which is the part I would insist on again.

details.value: Dropped 2 features that failed province-level review

title: Malaysia to Indonesia in under a minute
summary: Remittance took two days and cost 6%. The rails existed; nobody had joined them.
scope: Engineering manager · 11 engineers across KL and Jakarta
problem: Roughly 2.7 million Indonesians work in Malaysia and most send money home monthly. Correspondent banking made that a two-day, 6% transaction. DuitNow and QRIS both support cross-border in principle, but the FX, the AML screening and the two regulators' reporting formats had nobody owning the join.
approach: Treated it as three separate problems and resisted the pressure to ship them together: the payment rail, the FX book, and the compliance reporting. Built the rail first against a fixed internal FX rate so the hard part was isolated. Ran AML screening synchronously despite the latency cost - an asynchronous hold is worse for a migrant worker than an extra 400ms.
outcome: Live corridor at well under a minute end to end. The FX spread is where the honest caveat sits: we are cheaper than the incumbents and not as cheap as the mid-market rate implies, and we say so in the app.

details.label: Speed
details.value: 2 days → 48 seconds median end to end

details.label: Trade-off
details.value: Synchronous AML screening, +400ms, deliberate

details.value: 11 engineers, 2 regulators, 1 corridor at a time

title: From one backlog to three corridor pods
summary: Eleven engineers on one backlog meant every corridor waited on every other corridor.
scope: Engineering manager · 11 engineers, reporting to the CTO
problem: I inherited eleven engineers on one backlog and one on-call rotation. A regulator deadline on the Philippines corridor meant the Vietnam corridor's already-late work waited again, and two engineers had quietly stopped picking up anything with a date attached.
approach: Split into three corridor-owned pods of three to four engineers, each with its own on-call and its own roadmap, and stopped taking 'everyone helps everyone' requests from the top. Kept one shared platform pod for the FX and compliance code every corridor needed, so the split did not triplicate the parts that should not be triplicated. The first attempt split the pods by seniority, not by corridor, and every approval still routed through the senior pod anyway - reversed that after six weeks.
outcome: Corridors started shipping independently instead of queueing behind each other, and both engineers who had disengaged re-committed within the year - one of them now leads a pod.

title: The eKYC step that rejected legitimate customers
summary: A 22% rejection rate was being reported as fraud prevention working.
scope: Compliance PM · with risk, legal and 2 squads
problem: One in five onboarding attempts failed identity verification, and the dashboard framed that as blocked fraud. Sampling 400 rejections showed most were older MyKad cards with worn holograms, dark-skinned applicants failing the liveness check, and people in low light. That is not fraud prevention; that is a broken control with a flattering label.
approach: Got the metric renamed from 'fraud blocked' to 'verification failed', which was more than half the work - the name was why nobody had looked. Added a human review queue for the specific failure modes we could characterise, and required the vendor to report accuracy by skin tone before renewal. Two vendors declined to; that told us something.
outcome: Rejections fell without any measurable change in fraud. The vendor accuracy clause is now standard in our procurement.

title: A wallet that runs on a 1GB phone
summary: Our app was unusable on the devices most of our users actually own.
problem: Median device in our Cambodian user base has 1GB of RAM and Android Go. Our React Native bundle was 38MB and cold start was 11 seconds; the OS was killing the app in the background regularly, so users lost their session between scanning a QR and confirming. Crash-free rate on Go devices was 84%.
approach: Cut the bundle by removing three libraries we used for one function each, moved the Khmer font to a system fallback with a downloadable upgrade, and made the payment flow resumable from a persisted state so an OS kill is recoverable rather than fatal. Tested on a physical Go device every sprint, which sounds obvious and was not happening.
outcome: The app became usable on the hardware our users have. The persisted-state work mattered more than the bundle size, which was not what I expected going in.

details.label: Performance
details.value: Cold start 11s → 2.6s, bundle 38MB → 9MB

details.label: Reliability
details.value: Crash-free on Android Go 84% → 99.2%

details.label: Method
details.value: Every sprint tested on a physical 1GB Go device

details.label: Surprise
details.value: Resumable state mattered more than bundle size

title: Repayment schedules that match the harvest
summary: Monthly instalments made no sense for people paid twice a year.
problem: Smallholder rice farmers earn on a harvest cycle - two big inflows a year, very little between. We were charging monthly instalments, so delinquency spiked predictably in the pre-harvest months and we were treating a calendar artefact as credit risk. Collections costs were eating the margin.
approach: Modelled expected cash flow per farmer from crop, district and planting date, using BMKG rainfall data as a shift signal for harvest timing. Offered balloon repayment aligned to expected harvest with a small buffer. The forecast is wrong sometimes - late rains move a harvest by weeks - so the product has a no-penalty grace window rather than pretending to precision.
outcome: Delinquency stopped being seasonal and collections costs fell with it. The grace window gets used about 18% of the time, which is roughly how often our harvest timing is off.

details.label: Risk
details.value: Pre-harvest delinquency 19% → 6%

details.label: Cost
details.value: Collections cost per loan down 54%

details.label: Calibration
details.value: Grace window used 18% of the time - our forecast error rate

details.value: Crop, district, planting date, BMKG rainfall

title: Routing freight across an archipelago
summary: Road-graph routing is useless when the road is a ferry with a timetable.
scope: Team of 4 · I owned the multi-modal graph
problem: Java to Sulawesi is a road leg, a ferry with four sailings a day, and another road leg. Our engine treated the crossing as a fixed cost, so it produced plans that missed the last sailing and stranded a truck overnight. Dispatchers had stopped using the output and were planning by hand.
approach: Modelled ferries as timetabled edges rather than weighted ones, so a plan is only valid if the truck arrives before a real sailing. Added a penalty for the last sailing of the day because arriving with ten minutes of slack in Indonesian traffic is not a plan. Kept it explainable - dispatchers override anything they cannot see the reasoning for, so an unexplained optimum is worth nothing.
outcome: Dispatchers came back. Overnight strandings dropped sharply, which is the cost that actually hurt - a stranded truck is a driver in a hotel and a customer on the phone.

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Dispatcher plan acceptance 41% → 89%

details.label: Impact
details.value: Overnight strandings 63/month → 8/month

details.label: Performance
details.value: Multi-modal plan for 400 shipments in 3.4s

details.label: Design choice
details.value: Explainable over optimal - unexplained plans get overridden

title: An interface for someone wearing gloves in the rain
summary: We designed for a desk. The driver is on a motorcycle in a downpour.
problem: Pickup confirmation errors spiked in the wet season. Drivers were tapping a 44dp button with wet gloves on a rain-covered screen, one-handed, at a junction. The flow needed four taps and two of them were destructive if mis-hit.
approach: Rebuilt the flow to one large target plus voice confirmation in Bahasa Indonesia, removed every destructive action from the riding context entirely, and moved to high-contrast, large-type layouts that survive a wet screen and direct sun. Rode along for two weeks before drawing anything - most of what we needed to know is not visible from a usability lab.
outcome: Confirmation errors fell by more than half and the wet-season spike flattened. Voice confirmation gets used far more than we predicted, including in the dry season.

title: Predicting which COD parcels will not be paid for
summary: Cash on delivery is most of our volume and all of our loss.
problem: COD is about 71% of parcels in the Mekong Delta and the refusal rate was 8.9%. A refused parcel is two legs of delivery cost and a restocking fee for nothing. Operations wanted to charge a deposit, which would have killed the channel that makes the business work.
approach: Modelled refusal on order-level signals available before dispatch - address stability, order value against district median, time since the buyer's last completed order - deliberately excluding anything that looked like a proxy for income. High-risk parcels get a confirmation call before dispatch rather than a deposit demand. Kept a 5% unmanaged holdout permanently so we can still see the true baseline.
outcome: Refusals fell by nearly half without adding friction for the 90% of buyers who were always going to pay. Deposits never shipped.

title: Getting drivers to show up before riders did
summary: Classic cold start, except the supply side had been burned twice before.
scope: CPO · 28 people across product, ops and driver relations
problem: Two previous platforms had entered Metro Manila, subsidised heavily, and left. Drivers had learned that platform incentives are a trap, and no amount of sign-up bonus was going to move them - the objection was not the money, it was the expectation that the money would stop.
approach: Published a guaranteed minimum for twelve months in writing, with an early-termination payout if we withdrew it, and had the driver association review it before launch. That was an expensive, slow commitment and it was the only thing that worked. Sequenced by corridor rather than city-wide, so density arrived somewhere rather than thinly everywhere.
outcome: Corridor-level liquidity inside five months. The guarantee cost about ₱41M and replaced a subsidy budget that would have been larger and bought nothing durable.

title: Dispatch that keeps working when the towers go down
summary: Twenty typhoons a year, and our app needed four bars to do anything.
problem: During Typhoon Kristine, cell coverage across large parts of Bicol dropped for days. Our driver app could not even display an already-assigned job without a network call, so drivers with work in hand could not do it. That is the moment the platform matters most and it was the moment it was useless.
approach: Cached assigned jobs and the routing tiles for the driver's operating area on the device, queued completions locally, and made every screen render from the local store first with the network as an upgrade. Added a peer hand-off over Bluetooth for job transfers between drivers at a depot, which sounds exotic and is just how work actually moves when the towers are down.
outcome: Held up through two typhoons since. The Bluetooth hand-off gets used more in ordinary congestion than in disasters, which was not the design intent.

title: The Burmese text bug that was two bugs
summary: Half our users type Zawgyi, half type Unicode, and the bytes look similar enough to fool everyone.
problem: Myanmar has two incompatible encodings for the same script. Addresses entered on a Zawgyi phone render as nonsense on a Unicode one, so couriers were getting undeliverable addresses and we were blaming the customers. Our test data was all Unicode, so the suite could not see it.
approach: Built a fixture set in both encodings plus the mixed strings that appear when someone pastes between apps, and added detection-and-conversion assertions at every boundary - input, storage, label print, SMS. The hard part was the label printer, which silently substituted glyphs, so the assertion had to be on the rendered PNG rather than the string.
outcome: Undeliverable-address complaints fell sharply. The conversion layer is not perfect - a handful of mixed-encoding strings are genuinely ambiguous, and those now go to a human instead of to a courier.

details.value: Address-encoding defects 31/month → 2/month

details.label: Impact
details.value: Undeliverable-address complaints down 68%

title: Our model was good at English and we were measuring English
summary: Benchmarks said 0.87. Indonesian users said otherwise, and they were right.
problem: We sold a support assistant across six markets and evaluated it on translated English benchmarks. Real traffic is code-switched - Singlish, Bahasa rojak, Taglish - and tokenises terribly: an Indonesian query costs roughly 2.3x the tokens of its English equivalent, so it was also quietly the most expensive traffic we had.
approach: Built an eval set from real transcripts across all six markets, labelled by native speakers rather than translated, and reported per-language rather than in aggregate. The aggregate was fine; Vietnamese and Burmese were not. Also measured tokens per query per language, which turned a quality conversation into a unit-economics one and got it funded.
outcome: The per-language scorecard is now a release gate. Two markets were held back a quarter, which was the right call and an unpopular one.

details.label: Decision
details.value: Held 2 markets back a quarter

title: Cutting inference cost on languages the tokenizer hates
summary: Serving Indonesian cost more than serving English for no good reason.
scope: Team of 3 · I owned the serving path
problem: Our tokenizer was trained mostly on English text, so Southeast Asian scripts fragmented badly - Burmese averaged 4.1 tokens per word against English's 1.3. Cost per conversation in our largest market was roughly triple our smallest, and the pricing did not reflect that because we had never measured it.
approach: Extended the tokenizer vocabulary with SEA-language merges and continued pre-training rather than retraining from scratch, because the budget for scratch did not exist. Added per-language KV-cache sizing so a short Thai conversation does not reserve English-sized memory. Measured everything per language, per market, which nobody had done.
outcome: Cost per conversation dropped materially in the markets that needed it most. Quality moved slightly up rather than down, which was luck as much as design - vocabulary changes can easily go the other way.

details.label: Cost
details.value: Indonesian cost/conversation down 44%, Burmese down 58%

details.label: Performance
details.value: p95 first token 780ms → 410ms

details.label: Quality
details.value: Eval up 1.2 points - not the goal, and partly luck

details.label: Ownership
details.value: Vocabulary extension and per-language KV sizing

title: An assistant that knows when to be formal
summary: Getting the pronoun wrong in Javanese or Vietnamese is not a small mistake.
problem: Our assistant used one register per language. In Indonesian that reads as either stiff or rude depending on context; in Javanese and Vietnamese, where the pronoun encodes relative status, getting it wrong is genuinely offensive. Support tickets described the bot as 'kasar' - coarse - and we had been treating that as a tone preference.
approach: Worked with a linguist to define register tiers per language and tied them to context the product already knows - business account versus personal, first interaction versus tenth - rather than asking users to pick. Where the system cannot infer confidently, it uses the deferential form, because over-formality is a much cheaper error than under-formality.
outcome: Complaints about tone largely stopped. The defer-when-unsure rule is the part I would carry to any market with grammaticalised politeness.

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Tone complaints 140/month → 11/month

details.label: Task success
details.value: Conversation completion 68% → 84%

details.label: Rule
details.value: Defer when uncertain - over-formality is the cheaper error

details.label: Process
details.value: Register tiers defined with a linguist per language

title: Publishing the benchmark that made us look worse
summary: No public eval existed for our markets, so we built one and released it.
problem: Every model we evaluated - ours included - reported English-centric numbers. There was no shared benchmark for Bahasa Indonesia, Thai, Vietnamese, Tagalog or Burmese, which meant nobody in the region could compare anything honestly, and vendors could claim whatever they liked.
approach: Built a 4,200-item benchmark with native-speaker annotation in five languages, covering the code-switching and honorific handling that translated benchmarks miss entirely. Released it publicly under an open licence, including the results where our own model came third. Commercially that was argued about internally for a month.
outcome: Three other regional labs now report against it. Our own scores improved because the benchmark made the gaps legible, which is exactly the point of publishing it.

details.label: Adoption
details.value: 4,200 items, 5 languages, used by 3 external labs

details.label: Downstream
details.value: Our own Vietnamese score 0.61 → 0.79 in two quarters

details.label: Uncomfortable
details.value: Published results where we came third

details.label: Method
details.value: Native-speaker annotation, not machine translation

title: Referrals that do not send patients on a wasted trip
summary: A wrong referral costs a family a day of wages and a ferry ticket.
problem: BPJS requires a tiered referral, and our system let a puskesmas refer to a hospital that could not actually take the case - wrong specialty, no bed, or no BPJS contract for that procedure. In Bali that is an inconvenience. In Nusa Tenggara it is a boat, a day off work, and a family turned away at the door.
approach: Made hospital capability and live BPJS contract status a precondition for the referral rather than a lookup afterwards, which meant getting nine hospitals to maintain data they had no incentive to maintain. The unlock was showing each of them their own turned-away numbers. Took it through the clinical governance process rather than around it, which added two months and made it defensible.
outcome: Turned-away referrals fell substantially. The data-maintenance problem is not solved - it works because hospitals now see the cost, and that incentive needs re-making every year.

details.label: Primary metric
details.value: Turned-away referrals 23% → 6%

details.label: Patient impact
details.value: ~4,100 avoided wasted trips in year one

details.label: Fragile bit
details.value: Depends on hospitals maintaining data - incentive needs renewing

details.label: Governance
details.value: Through clinical governance, +2 months, deliberate

title: Consultations that work on a 2G connection
summary: Video telehealth excluded exactly the patients who most needed it.
problem: Our telehealth product was video-first. In the districts with the worst doctor-to-patient ratios, bandwidth will not carry video, so the product was best where it was needed least. Consultation abandonment outside major cities was 52%.
approach: Added an audio-only path that is not a degraded fallback but a first-class flow, with structured symptom capture beforehand so the doctor arrives informed and the call can be shorter. Store-and-forward for images - a photo of a rash uploads over two minutes on 2G and does not need a live stream. Progressive degradation is automatic and visible, so nobody wonders whether it is broken.
outcome: Rural completion came up close to urban levels. The structured pre-capture turned out to shorten urban video consultations too, which was an accident.

details.label: Reliability
details.value: Rural consultation completion 48% → 86%

details.label: Scale
details.value: Works down to 64kbps; 31% of consults are audio-only

details.label: Unexpected
details.value: Pre-capture cut urban video consults by 4 minutes too

details.label: Ownership
details.value: Audio path, store-and-forward, degradation signalling

title: Claim forms an 70-year-old can finish alone
summary: Three languages, two scripts, and a user base whose eyesight is not what it was.
problem: Health claims skew old. Ours was a 34-field form in English with Malay and Mandarin toggles that reset your progress. 61% of claims over-60 were completed by a family member instead of the policyholder, which is a privacy problem as much as a usability one.
approach: Cut to 11 fields by pulling the rest from records we already held, kept language state across the whole session, and set a 18px floor with real Malay, Mandarin and Tamil typesetting rather than a font that only looks right in Latin. Tested with people over 65 in their own homes, on their own phones, with their own reading glasses.
outcome: Unassisted completion more than doubled. The field reduction did most of the work; the typography did the rest.

details.label: Task success
details.value: Unassisted completion over-60 39% → 81%

details.label: Effort
details.value: 34 fields → 11; median time 19min → 6min

details.label: Accessibility
details.value: 18px floor, WCAG AA, 3 languages typeset properly

details.label: Process
details.value: Tested in-home with 22 people over 65

title: Dengue signal from 1,700 barangay health stations
summary: The data existed. It arrived as scanned paper, six weeks late.
problem: Barangay health stations reported case counts on paper, couriered to a city office and keyed in. By the time a cluster was visible in the national numbers it was six weeks old, which is several dengue generations. Digital reporting had been attempted twice and abandoned because the stations have intermittent power, let alone connectivity.
approach: Built around SMS rather than an app, because a feature phone with a topped-up SIM is the one piece of technology every station has. Structured short codes, with a weekly reconciliation against the paper record so the data lineage survives an audit. Built in the assumption that some stations will not report some weeks, and modelled that absence explicitly instead of imputing it away.
outcome: Detection lag collapsed from weeks to days and two clusters were caught early enough to matter. Coverage sits at 83%, not 100%, and the dashboard shows which stations are missing rather than hiding it in an average.

details.label: Detection lag
details.value: 6 weeks → 4 days median

details.label: Impact
details.value: 2 clusters caught early enough for vector response

details.label: Coverage
details.value: 83% of stations - shown explicitly, never imputed

details.label: Design choice
details.value: SMS, not an app - power and connectivity are not assumptions

title: Proving a palm oil block was not deforested
summary: EU regulation needed plot-level provenance we had never had to produce.
problem: The EU Deforestation Regulation requires geolocated proof that a shipment did not come from land cleared after 2020. Our mills buy from thousands of smallholders whose plots were recorded as a village name. Without plot-level provenance the European contracts were simply gone.
approach: Combined Sentinel-2 change detection with GPS plot boundaries captured by field agents, and - the part that mattered - built an explicit confidence grade per plot rather than a binary compliant flag. A plot with cloud-obscured imagery for three months is not 'compliant', it is 'unknown', and saying so is what makes the rest credible with an auditor.
outcome: The European contracts held. About 11% of plots sit in 'unknown' and go through manual verification, which is expensive and honest.

details.label: Business impact
details.value: Retained €18M of EU contracts at risk

details.label: Coverage
details.value: 94% of supply traced to plot, 11% graded 'unknown'

details.label: Design choice
details.value: Confidence grades, not a binary compliant flag

details.label: Data
details.value: Sentinel-2 change detection + 24,000 GPS plot boundaries

title: A catch log fishers actually keep
summary: Every previous version assumed a dry hand and a spare minute.
problem: Sustainable-quota work needs catch data and the data did not exist. Two earlier apps had been built and abandoned: both wanted species, weight and coordinates typed in at sea, on a wet boat, by someone with both hands occupied. Compliance was under 5%.
approach: Moved logging off the boat entirely and onto the landing site, where the catch is already being weighed and sorted and someone is already writing numbers down. Designed around that existing moment rather than inventing a new one: a shared tablet at the weighing station, species by photo, weight from the scale over Bluetooth. Went out on boats for a week first, which is mostly how we learned the app should not be on boats.
outcome: Compliance went from negligible to usable. The lesson I keep is that the best interface was the one that removed itself from the hardest moment.

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Catch logging compliance 4% → 71%

details.label: Data quality
details.value: Weight entry error 22% → 1.8% via scale integration

details.label: Method
details.value: A week at sea, then a decision to leave the boat alone

details.label: Honest bit
details.value: Two previous apps failed doing it the obvious way

title: The reef data that changed who we were building for
summary: We were designing for marine scientists. The people with the knowledge were the fishers.
problem: Our monitoring platform was scoped for research institutions. Six months in, data coverage was thin and seasonal - scientists visit, fishers live there. The assumption that scientific users were the primary users had never been tested; it came from who was in the room when the product was scoped.
approach: Spent seven months across six coastal villages, including three full lunar cycles because reef access and fishing patterns follow tides, not calendars. Found detailed, precise local knowledge of reef condition held by people who had never been asked and had no reason to trust an outside platform with it. Co-designed the data-sharing terms with the village councils rather than presenting them.
outcome: The platform's primary user changed. Coverage went from seasonal to continuous. The co-designed terms took four months and are the reason any of it works.

details.label: Decision changed
details.value: Primary user redefined from researchers to fishers

details.label: Downstream
details.value: Reef observations 340/year → 11,000/year

details.label: Method
details.value: 6 villages, 3 lunar cycles, council co-design of data terms

details.label: Cost
details.value: 4 months negotiating terms - non-negotiable in hindsight

title: Regional data residency without three copies of everything
summary: Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore all want the data to stay put.
problem: PP 71 in Indonesia, Vietnam's Decree 53 and customer contracts in Singapore all constrained where personal data may live. The proposed answer was three full stacks, which triples the cost and, worse, triples the number of places a deploy can be subtly different.
approach: Split services by whether they touch personal data rather than by geography. Roughly two thirds do not, and those stay single-region. The rest run per-region from one Terraform module with region as a variable, so a deploy is identical everywhere by construction. Made data classification a required field on every service manifest, which was the unpopular part and the reason it holds.
outcome: Compliant in all three jurisdictions on about 40% of the projected cost. The classification requirement has caught four services that would have quietly leaked personal data across a border.

details.label: Cost
details.value: ~40% of the projected three-stack cost

details.label: Reliability
details.value: 4 cross-border data leaks caught before shipping

details.label: Scope
details.value: 29 services, 3 jurisdictions, 1 Terraform module

details.label: Unpopular bit
details.value: Data classification required on every service manifest

title: Finding $380k a year in cross-region traffic
summary: The bill said compute. The bill was wrong.
problem: Cloud spend was growing faster than traffic and every team was told to optimise compute. Nobody had attributed egress, which turned out to be 31% of the bill - services in Singapore chatting with a database in Jakarta, thousands of times a second, because a config default had never been revisited.
approach: Made cost visible per service before asking anyone to change anything, because a team cannot optimise a number it cannot see. Then co-located the chattiest pairs and added a read replica rather than rewriting call patterns, which would have been architecturally purer and taken a year. Left a deliberately ugly dashboard showing egress per service on the wall.
outcome: Spend fell and, more usefully, teams started making regional placement decisions on their own. The dashboard did more than the migration did.

details.label: Cost
details.value: $380k/year, egress from 31% → 9% of the bill

details.label: Reliability
details.value: p95 cross-service latency 180ms → 40ms as a side effect

details.label: Method
details.value: Made cost visible per service before asking for changes

details.label: Trade-off
details.value: Co-location and a replica over a year-long rewrite

title: Knowing what is actually in the build
summary: Nine countries of engineering contractors, and no inventory of our dependencies.
problem: A regional client asked which of our services included a specific compromised npm package. It took eleven days to answer, and the answer was partly a guess. With contract teams across nine countries committing to 40 repos, nobody could say what shipped.
approach: Generated an SBOM on every build and stored it against the deployed artefact, so the question becomes a query rather than an investigation. Added provenance attestation so a build can be traced to a commit and a runner. Deliberately did not start with blocking policy - an inventory nobody trusts is worse than no policy, so the first six months were just making it accurate.
outcome: The same question now takes under a minute. Blocking policy came later, once the inventory had earned enough trust that a block was believed rather than bypassed.

details.label: Response time
details.value: 'Which services include X?' 11 days → 45 seconds

details.label: Coverage
details.value: 40 repos, 9 countries, 100% of production artefacts

details.label: Sequencing
details.value: Six months of accuracy before any blocking policy

details.label: Provenance
details.value: Every artefact traceable to commit and runner

title: From eleven days to a first commit, to one
summary: Hiring across five countries exposed how much our setup relied on asking someone.
problem: Median time to first merged commit was eleven days. The setup guide was accurate in 2022. In one office that cost you a morning of tapping someone on the shoulder; for a new hire in Da Nang or Cebu with a four-hour overlap, it cost a week and a half and a lot of dignity.
approach: Made the environment reproducible from a single command using devcontainers, and - the part that actually mattered - made the CI job run the same setup script, so a broken setup breaks the build and gets fixed within hours instead of silently rotting. Wrote the docs in English only, deliberately: mixed-language docs had drifted apart and the English one was always the current one.
outcome: First commit inside a day, and the gap between the headquarters office and everywhere else closed. The CI-runs-the-setup-script trick is the whole trick.

details.label: Delivery
details.value: Time to first merged commit 11 days → 1 day

details.label: Equity
details.value: Remote-office gap 6 days → 0.5 days

details.label: Key trick
details.value: CI runs the setup script, so rot breaks the build

details.label: Deliberate
details.value: English-only docs - mixed-language versions drifted

title: Testing a live game on the networks people actually have
summary: Our QA lab had fibre. Our players had a shared 4G cell at 8pm.
problem: Match desync complaints clustered in Indonesia and the Philippines every evening and we could not reproduce any of it. The studio tested on office fibre, so the entire class of failure - 300ms jitter, 4% packet loss, NAT churn as phones hop cells - was invisible to us.
approach: Built a network-shaping harness into CI with profiles taken from real player telemetry rather than textbook numbers, including the evening-peak profile that was causing the complaints. Added a desync detector that captures a state hash so a failure gives us a reproduction rather than a report. Ran the full matrix nightly instead of per-PR, because it takes 40 minutes and honesty about that is better than a suite people skip.
outcome: Desync complaints fell by most of what they were. The evening profile now catches things before release that we previously learned about from a subreddit.

details.label: Escape rate
details.value: Desync reports 210/week → 34/week

details.label: Reproduction
details.value: Desyncs with a usable repro 12% → 89%

details.label: Profiles
details.value: Built from player telemetry, not textbook impairment numbers

details.label: Trade-off
details.value: Nightly, not per-PR - 40 minutes, and we said so

title: An economy for players who will never spend $50
summary: Western monetisation benchmarks were telling us our players were worthless.
problem: ARPU benchmarks from US and EU titles framed our Southeast Asian players as low value, and the roadmap was drifting toward harder paywalls to close the gap. Meanwhile session frequency and D30 retention were well above those same benchmarks. We were optimising against the wrong denominator.
approach: Reframed on lifetime value against a two-year horizon rather than 30-day ARPU, which changes the answer completely for a player base that plays daily for years and spends a dollar at a time. Tested small, frequent, locally-priced bundles against a single premium tier. Ran it as a proper holdout by market so the result was not confounded by a regional festival.
outcome: Revenue rose while the paywall got softer, which is the outcome I would not have predicted. Retention was unchanged, which mattered - the alternative plan would have traded it away.

details.label: Result vs control
details.value: Revenue per player +34% over 24 weeks (n = 220k)

details.label: Retention held
details.value: D30 unchanged at 41% - the thing we refused to trade

details.label: Reframe
details.value: 2-year LTV, not 30-day ARPU

details.label: Pricing
details.value: Local price points, small and frequent, not one premium tier

title: Publishing salary bands across six countries
summary: Location-based pay was defensible on a spreadsheet and indefensible in a room.
scope: Head of talent · with finance and the exec team
problem: We paid by location, so two engineers doing identical work with identical output could differ by 2.6x between Singapore and Da Nang. Offer acceptance in Vietnam and the Philippines was 41% and our best regional candidates were leaving for fully-remote Western roles. The spreadsheet said we were being efficient.
approach: Moved to role-and-level bands with a cost-of-living adjustment that is published and bounded at 1.4x rather than unbounded, and published the whole band structure internally. That cost real money and was argued about for a quarter. Nobody had their pay cut - closing the gap upward is the only version that does not destroy trust.
outcome: Acceptance rose sharply and regional attrition fell. Payroll went up about 9%, which was the price and was known going in.

details.label: Hiring
details.value: Offer acceptance in VN/PH 41% → 78%

details.label: Retention
details.value: Regional attrition 24% → 11%

details.label: Cost
details.value: Payroll +9%, budgeted and approved up front

details.label: Principle
details.value: Closed the gap upward - nobody's pay was cut

title: Growth on the channels Vietnam actually uses
summary: Our whole playbook assumed a Meta and WhatsApp market. Vietnam is neither.
problem: The regional playbook was Meta ads into a WhatsApp onboarding flow. In Vietnam the shippers we needed live on Zalo, and our CAC was 3.1x the regional average because we were buying attention in the wrong place and then asking people to install something else.
approach: Rebuilt acquisition around Zalo Official Account with onboarding completed inside the chat, so there is no app install before the first job is booked. Measured with geo holdouts rather than platform-reported attribution, because self-reported numbers from any ad platform are a marketing document. Kept a small Meta spend as a control rather than cutting it entirely.
outcome: CAC came down below the regional average and the channel held for six months. The in-chat onboarding did more than the media shift - removing the install was the actual unlock.

details.label: Efficiency
details.value: CAC ₫2.9M → ₫840k, below regional average

details.label: Result vs control
details.value: Activation 27% → 61% with in-chat onboarding

details.label: Method
details.value: Geo holdouts, not platform-reported attribution

details.label: Finding
details.value: Removing the app install beat the media shift

title: The stock forecasting service we switched off
summary: Technically fine, genuinely useless, and we killed it after four months live.
problem: Sellers ran out of fast-moving stock and we assumed a forecasting problem. I built a per-SKU demand service with seasonality, promotions and a warm cache, and it was accurate - MAPE around 14% on top-50 SKUs, which is respectable.
approach: Shipped it as a reorder suggestion on the stock screen. Instrumented acceptance. Over four months, 6% of suggestions were acted on. Sat with fourteen sellers and found the constraint was never knowing what to reorder - it was cash on the day the supplier's truck arrives. A perfect forecast does not help someone who cannot pay for the stock this week.
outcome: We switched it off and put the team on supplier credit terms instead, which is now a real product line. The forecasting code is deleted; I would rather that than leave it running to protect the decision to build it.

details.label: Accuracy
details.value: MAPE 14% on top-50 SKUs - the model was fine

details.label: Adoption
details.value: 6% of suggestions acted on over 4 months

details.label: Outcome
details.value: Switched off and deleted; team moved to supplier credit

details.label: Lesson
details.value: We validated the model and never validated the constraint

title: Making the accessible component the easy one
summary: Four designers, three codebases and a contrast ratio nobody was checking.
problem: We had an accessibility standard written down and roughly a third of shipped screens met it. Not because anyone disagreed with it - because meeting it meant remembering a rule while doing something else, and the default component did not.
approach: Stopped writing guidance and changed the defaults. Rebuilt the component library so the accessible version is the one you get by typing the obvious name, moved contrast and target-size checks into the PR pipeline as a failing check rather than a warning, and deleted the variants that let you build an inaccessible screen without meaning to.
outcome: Compliance became a non-event because the easy path is now the compliant one. The deletions caused a fortnight of friction and were the load-bearing part.

details.label: Compliance
details.value: Screens meeting AA 34% → 96%

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Library coverage 41% → 88% of shipped UI

details.label: Method
details.value: Changed defaults and deleted variants, not more guidance

details.label: Friction
details.value: A fortnight of complaints about the deletions - worth it

title: The outage that was a retry storm we built ourselves
summary: Ninety minutes of failed payments, caused by our own resilience logic.
problem: A 400ms latency bump in an upstream acquirer turned into a 90-minute total payment outage. Every service had a sensible-looking retry policy, and stacked together they multiplied the load on a degraded dependency by roughly 27x. Each individual policy had passed review.
approach: Ran the postmortem without naming the team whose config was the proximate trigger, because the configuration was reasonable in isolation and the failure was in the absence of a global view. Added budgeted retries with jitter and a circuit breaker at the boundary, and - the durable change - a load test that specifically simulates a slow dependency rather than a dead one.
outcome: The same upstream degraded twice since with no customer impact. The slow-dependency test has caught two similar patterns before release.

details.label: Reliability
details.value: 2 subsequent upstream degradations, zero customer impact

details.label: Root cause
details.value: Stacked retries multiplied load on a degraded dependency 27x

details.label: Durable change
details.value: Load test for a slow dependency, not just a dead one

details.label: Culture
details.value: Postmortem named no team - the gap was the global view

title: Refunds a merchant can issue without calling support
summary: Every refund went through a support agent, and most of them did not need to.
problem: Merchants had no way to refund a customer themselves, so 3,400 support tickets a month were someone reading a transaction ID over the phone. Support was the bottleneck and merchants looked unreliable to their own customers while they waited.
approach: Designed self-service refunds with the risky cases still routed to a human: partial refunds over a threshold, anything past 30 days, and any merchant under 60 days old. The hard part was the confirmation - a refund is irreversible and the previous design of an irreversible action in this product had a 12% mis-tap rate, so we used an explicit amount re-entry rather than a checkbox.
outcome: Most refunds now never touch support, and merchant-side resolution time went from hours to under a minute. Mis-taps did not materialise.

details.label: Support load
details.value: Refund tickets 3,400/month → 410/month

details.label: Task success
details.value: Merchant resolution time 4.2h → 48s median

details.label: Safety
details.value: Amount re-entry, not a checkbox; mis-taps under 0.3%

details.label: Deliberately kept
details.value: High-value, aged and new-merchant refunds stay human

title: Rearranging a warehouse with a solver and a tape measure
summary: Pickers were walking 14km a shift because the layout was five years stale.
scope: Engineer · with the Surabaya warehouse team
problem: Pick times had crept up 40% over two years as the product mix changed and the slotting never did. Fast-movers were at the back because that is where they were when the warehouse opened.
approach: Built a re-slotting solver on pick-frequency and affinity, then did the unglamorous half: walked the floor with the supervisors and let them veto anything that broke how they actually work. They vetoed about a fifth of the suggestions - heavy items away from the ramp, chilled goods kept together - and every veto was right for a reason the model had no way to know.
outcome: Walking distance and pick times both fell hard. I would not run this again without the veto pass; the solver alone would have produced a layout the team could not use.

details.label: Performance
details.value: Picker walking distance 14km → 6.2km per shift

details.label: Throughput
details.value: Picks per hour 62 → 104

details.label: Method
details.value: Supervisors vetoed ~20% of suggestions, all correctly

details.label: Lesson
details.value: The solver was half the work; the floor walk was the other half

title: Catching mule account networks
summary: Rules caught individuals. The money moved through networks of them.
problem: Scam proceeds were being layered through rings of mule accounts, each of which looked ordinary in isolation. Our rules scored accounts independently and were structurally incapable of seeing a ring. Reported losses were climbing and the recovery window is measured in hours.
approach: Built a graph over transfer patterns, shared devices and registration fingerprints, scoring communities rather than accounts. Held out chronologically, not randomly - a random split leaked future structure and flattered the model by about eight points. Kept a human in the loop before any freeze, because freezing a legitimate account is a serious harm and false positives here are not symmetrical with false negatives.
outcome: Ring detection went from effectively nothing to usable within the recovery window. Roughly one in nine flagged communities is cleared by review, which is the cost of not freezing people automatically.

details.label: Eval vs baseline
details.value: Ring recall 0.08 → 0.63 at fixed precision

details.label: Production
details.value: ~Rp 31B of layered funds held within the recovery window

details.label: Guardrail
details.value: Human review before any freeze; 11% of flags cleared

details.label: Method
details.value: Chronological hold-out - random split leaked ~8 points

title: Our retrieval scored 0.88 and returned the wrong document
summary: The eval set was written by the people who built the system.
problem: Offline retrieval metrics were strong and support tickets said otherwise. The eval set had been assembled from questions we already knew the corpus answered, which measures the corpus rather than the system.
approach: Rebuilt the eval from real user queries including the third we had failed - the half everyone skips, because labelling failures is slow and unrewarding. Split by query type and found the aggregate was hiding near-total failure on multi-hop questions.
outcome: The honest score came in far lower, which was the point. Fixing multi-hop specifically moved the real number more than six weeks of embedding tuning had.

details.label: Eval vs baseline
details.value: Honest recall@5 0.88 claimed → 0.61 measured → 0.79 fixed

details.label: Production
details.value: Wrong-document tickets down 64%

details.label: Data
details.value: 1,200 real queries including 360 known failures

details.label: Method
details.value: Reported by query type - the aggregate was the problem

title: Onboarding 6,000 drivers without a background-check bottleneck
summary: Compliance took nine days and we were losing half our applicants inside it.
scope: CPO · with legal, ops and 1 squad
problem: NBI clearance, LTO licence verification and our own checks ran sequentially and took nine days. 54% of applicants dropped out during the wait, usually to a competitor who had started them on a provisional basis.
approach: Parallelised every check that could legally run concurrently and introduced a provisional status with a restricted job set - shorter trips, cash-free only - for the window where the slow checks are still pending. Legal was, correctly, the hardest conversation; the restriction set is what made it defensible.
outcome: Drop-out during onboarding fell by most of what it was. Two provisional drivers failed a later check in the first year and were removed within a day, which is the residual risk we accepted in writing.

details.label: Hiring
details.value: Applicant drop-out during checks 54% → 12%

details.label: Speed
details.value: Time to first job 9 days → 26 hours

details.label: Residual risk
details.value: 2 provisional drivers failed later checks, removed in <24h

details.label: Design
details.value: Restricted job set is what made provisional status defensible

title: A service catalogue people actually update
summary: Our previous catalogue was accurate for about six weeks.
problem: Nobody could answer who owns a service, what it depends on, or whether it is in the on-call rotation, without asking in Slack. A wiki catalogue had been tried and rotted, as wiki catalogues do, because updating it was a separate act of goodwill.
approach: Generated the catalogue from things teams already maintain - the deploy manifest, the on-call schedule, the repo - so it cannot drift without something else breaking first. Added exactly one required field they did not already keep, data classification, and accepted that one field's worth of friction. Refused the temptation to add the other twelve fields people asked for.
outcome: Still accurate two years on, which is the only metric that matters for a catalogue. The restraint about extra fields is the reason.

details.label: Accuracy
details.value: Still accurate at 24 months; the wiki version lasted 6 weeks

details.label: Delivery
details.value: 'Who owns this?' from a Slack thread to a lookup

details.label: Restraint
details.value: One new required field. Twelve were requested.

details.label: Design
details.value: Generated from artefacts teams already maintain

title: Cutting pages by 80% by deleting alerts
summary: On-call was waking up nine times a week and fixing almost nothing.
problem: Median 9.2 pages per on-call week, of which about 15% led to any action. Two engineers had left citing on-call. Every alert had been added by someone reasonable after some incident, and nobody had ever been given permission to remove one.
approach: Audited every alert against a single question - if this fires at 3am, is there something a human must do right now? Anything that failed went to a dashboard or a ticket. Deleted 140 of 190 alerts. Got explicit written sign-off from each service owner beforehand, because deleting alerts is a trust exercise long before it is a technical one.
outcome: Pages dropped hard and actionability went up, which is the pairing that matters. Time to acknowledge halved, because a page now means something.

details.label: On-call load
details.value: 9.2 pages/week → 1.8

details.label: Actionability
details.value: Pages requiring human action 15% → 71%

details.label: Response
details.value: Median time to acknowledge 11min → 5min

details.label: Method
details.value: Deleted 140 of 190 alerts, with written owner sign-off

title: Queue numbers for a clinic that opens at 5am
summary: Patients queued from before dawn for a number, then waited all day anyway.
problem: Patients arrived at 5am to queue for a paper number for a consultation that might happen at 2pm. Our booking feature had been live for a year with 4% uptake. The assumption was low digital literacy; the reality was that a booked slot was not honoured, so the queue was still the only thing that worked.
approach: Fixed the operational side before touching the app: worked with clinic staff to reserve a genuine share of slots for bookings and to hold them. Only then did the booking feature mean anything. Kept the paper queue running in parallel and did not try to retire it, because a system that excludes people without a phone is not a health system.
outcome: Uptake rose once bookings were real. Average wait fell by hours. The paper queue is still there and should be.

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Booking uptake 4% → 47% across 6 puskesmas

details.label: Patient impact
details.value: Median wait 6.1h → 1.4h

details.label: Sequencing
details.value: Fixed slot-holding operationally before touching the app

details.label: Deliberately kept
details.value: Paper queue retained - excluding the phone-less is not an option

title: Halal traceability as a first-class feature
summary: A compliance checkbox for us; a market-access requirement for our customers.
problem: Indonesian and Malaysian food manufacturers need auditable halal chain-of-custody, and Indonesia's mandatory certification deadlines were approaching. We had a certificate-upload field. Customers were maintaining the real record in parallel spreadsheets, which meant our ERP was not the system of record for the thing that decides whether they can sell.
approach: Modelled halal status as a property of a batch that propagates through production, so a non-halal input contaminates its outputs automatically rather than relying on someone remembering. Ran it with five design partners including two who failed an audit during the project - those two taught us more than the three who passed.
outcome: The parallel spreadsheets went away for the design partners. Audit preparation went from weeks to days, which is the number the customers quote back to us.

details.label: Business impact
details.value: Audit prep 3 weeks → 2 days for design partners

details.label: Adoption
details.value: Parallel spreadsheets retired at 5 of 5 partners

details.label: Method
details.value: Propagating batch property, not a certificate field

details.label: Learning
details.value: The 2 partners who failed an audit taught us most

title: The migration we rolled back at 60%
summary: Nine months of work, stopped four weeks in, and it was the right call.
duration: 9 months build, 4 weeks live, 1 day to roll back
scope: Team of 5 · I owned the cutover plan
problem: We were moving the ledger from a row-per-balance model to event sourcing for auditability. Built well, tested hard, dual-ran for six weeks with reconciliation. At 60% of traffic, month-end close took 9 hours instead of 40 minutes - replaying a month of events at our volume was a workload nobody had load-tested because we had only ever tested the write path.
approach: Rolled back inside a day, which only worked because we had kept the old path warm and had not yet migrated historical data. Wrote it up internally with the specific gap named: we tested the thing we were building and not the thing the finance team does once a month. Rebuilt with periodic snapshots and re-ran the whole dual-run before trying again.
outcome: Second attempt shipped six months later and close runs in 22 minutes. I would do the rollback the same way; the mistake was four weeks earlier, in what we chose to load-test.

details.label: Rollback
details.value: 60% of traffic reverted in under a day, zero data loss

details.label: Second attempt
details.value: Shipped 6 months later; close 9h → 22min

details.label: Root cause
details.value: Load-tested the write path, never the monthly close

details.label: What saved it
details.value: Old path kept warm; historical data not yet migrated

title: One component library for a phone on a handlebar
summary: Driver and shipper apps had drifted into two different products.
problem: Two apps, two teams, two sets of components that looked similar and behaved differently. A driver switching between our apps got different gesture meanings for the same swipe, which in a moving-vehicle context is not a consistency nicety.
approach: Built one library with explicit context variants - 'in-motion' components have larger targets, higher contrast and no destructive actions, and that is enforced by the component rather than by a guideline. Motion tokens were the surprise: the same 300ms transition that reads as polished on a desk reads as sluggish when you are waiting at a junction, so in-motion variants run faster.
outcome: Gesture inconsistencies across the apps went to zero and shipping a driver-facing screen got noticeably faster. The in-motion variant idea has outlived the project.

details.label: Consistency
details.value: Cross-app gesture conflicts 14 → 0

details.label: Delivery
details.value: Driver-facing screen build time down 45%

details.label: Idea that lasted
details.value: In-motion variants: bigger targets, faster motion, no destructive actions

details.label: Enforcement
details.value: In the component, not in a guideline
